title: Linked lists

story.title: The play queue of a music app
story.summary: You build the play queue of a music app. Listeners tap Play next, remove songs and jump around, and the queue has to stay fast when it holds thousands of songs.

uses.title: Undo history in an editor
uses.body: Each edit links back to the one before it, so undo steps back along the chain.

uses.title: Browser back and forward
uses.body: Each page links to the one before and the one after, so back and forward move one link.

uses.title: LRU cache in front of a database
uses.body: A hash map finds an entry and a doubly linked list orders entries by recent use, so touching one relinks a few nodes.

uses.title: The OS list of running processes
uses.body: Starting or ending a process relinks its neighbours and leaves the rest of the list alone.

whenNot: Arrays usually win for indexed reads and for visiting every item. Their items sit side by side in memory, so the CPU cache loads many at once and index lookup is O(1). Choose a linked list when you often insert or remove in the middle at a position you already hold.

outcomes.explain-nodes-and-links: Explain how nodes and links make up a linked list
outcomes.traverse-from-head: Traverse a linked list from its head with a pointer
outcomes.insert-in-constant-time: Insert a node after a known node in O(1)
outcomes.delete-by-relinking: Delete a node by relinking around it
outcomes.compare-with-arrays: Compare the costs of linked lists and arrays

the-problem.title: Play next freezes the app
the-problem.caption: Your play queue is an array, and a listener taps Play next on Glow. Glow goes right after Intro, so Echo, Drift and Pulse each shift one cell to the right. On a 10,000-song queue the app freezes on that tap.
the-problem.keyIdea: Inserting in the middle of an array shifts every item behind it.

a-node.title: A song becomes a node
a-node.caption: You store each song in its own box. A [[node]] holds two things: a value and a link called next. Here the node holds Intro, and its next points nowhere yet.
a-node.keyIdea: A node is a value plus a link to the next node.

linking-songs.title: Songs joined into a queue
linking-songs.caption: You add Echo, Drift and Pulse, then link each node to the one after it. Following the links takes you from Intro to Pulse. The last node's next is null, which marks the end of the [[linked-list]].

the-head.title: The head starts the queue
the-head.caption: The queue needs one more thing: the [[head]], a reference to its first node. You set the head to Intro, the one node no other node links to. From the head, the links reach every other song.

now-playing-pointer.title: A pointer marks the playing song
now-playing-pointer.caption: A [[pointer]] is a labelled marker that refers to one node. You place now-playing on Intro, the song playing right now. When the song ends, the marker moves along its next link.

traversal.title: Walking the queue
traversal.caption: To fill the Up next list, you walk the queue. A cursor starts on Intro and follows next to Echo, Drift and Pulse. Pulse's next is null, so the walk stops. Visiting the nodes one after another like this is [[traversal]].

play-next.title: Play next links a new song in
play-next.caption: You create the node Glow and link its next to Echo, the song after the one playing. Only then do you link Intro's next to Glow. Two links change and no song moves, so the cost does not depend on the length of the queue.
play-next.keyIdea: Link the new node forward first, then link the old node to it.

remove-from-queue.title: Remove by relinking
remove-from-queue.caption: The listener removes Echo. You point prev at Glow, the song before it, and link Glow's next to Drift. Nothing points at Echo any more, so you remove it. The other songs never move.
remove-from-queue.keyIdea: To remove a node, relink the node before it past it.

jump-to-song.title: Jumping to a song takes a walk
jump-to-song.caption: A queue has no index to jump to. To reach index 3, which holds Pulse, the cursor starts at the head and follows next three times. Song 500 is 499 links from the head, so reaching index k takes k moves.
jump-to-song.keyIdea: A linked list has no index: reaching position k means walking k links.

arrays-vs-lists.title: Arrays and linked lists side by side
arrays-vs-lists.caption: The array reaches Pulse in one jump by index, while the list walks three links. The list plays a song next by changing two links, while the array shifts every song behind it. Showing Up next visits every song once on both.
arrays-vs-lists.keyIdea: Pick the structure by the operation you repeat most.

where-you-meet-it.title: Where you will meet it
where-you-meet-it.caption: Linked lists run inside the systems listed below, from your editor's undo to the operating system. Each keeps its items in order and changes them at a spot it already holds. The note under them says when an array is the better pick.

reverse-preview.title: Next up: reverse the queue
reverse-preview.caption: In Practice you reverse a list in place with three pointers: prev, current and next. Before the first move, prev is null, current sits on the head and next is one node ahead. You redirect each node's link, one node at a time.

what-a-node-links-to.prompt: Intro is a single node. For Echo to come after it, what must Intro hold besides its song name?

options.next-link: A link to the next node, because the queue continues by following it
options.copy-of-next: A copy of the next song's name, because the name tells you which song follows
options.position-number: Its position number, because the queue finds each song by position
options.nothing-extra: Nothing more, because nodes sit side by side like array cells

what-a-node-links-to.explanation: Intro holds a link to the next node, called next, and the queue continues by following it. A copy of Echo's name says nothing about where Echo is, and two songs can share a name. Nodes have no position number, because a list finds a node by walking the links. Nodes do not sit side by side in memory, so without a link nothing connects Intro to Echo.

which-song-is-head.prompt: The queue has no head yet. Select the song the head should refer to.
which-song-is-head.explanation: The head is Intro, because no link leads into Intro, so only the head can lead you there. If the head referred to Drift, you would lose Intro and Echo. If it referred to Pulse, the last node, you could reach nothing else, since its next is null.

where-the-walk-lands.prompt: A cursor starts on the song now-playing marks and follows next one link at a time. After two moves, which song is it on?
where-the-walk-lands.explanation: The cursor is on Drift: the first move reaches Echo and the second reaches Drift. It does not stop on Echo, because a move counts only when you follow a link. It does not reach Pulse either, since that takes a third move. Links only point forward, so the cursor never goes back.

first-link-for-play-next.prompt: A listener taps Play next on Glow while Intro is playing. Which link do you set first?

options.new-to-next: Glow's next, set to Echo, because Glow must know what follows it before anything points at it
options.current-to-new: Intro's next, set to Glow, because the playing song must lead to Glow
options.new-to-current: Glow's next, set to Intro, because Glow must know where it came from
options.either-order: Either one first, because both links are set in the end

first-link-for-play-next.explanation: You set Glow's next to Echo first. If you link Intro to Glow first, nothing points to Echo any more, and Echo, Drift and Pulse are lost. If you set Glow's next back to Intro, Intro leads to Glow and Glow leads back to Intro, so the queue loops and Echo can no longer be reached. The order matters because Intro's old next is the only reference to the rest of the queue.

song-before-the-removed.prompt: The listener removes Echo from the queue. Select the song whose next link must change.
song-before-the-removed.explanation: Glow's next must change, because Glow is the node that points at Echo. Intro's next already points at Glow and stays as it is. Drift's next points at Pulse, so it stays too. You link Glow straight to Drift, and Echo drops out.

cost-of-reaching-index-k.prompt: The listener taps the song at index k, where the head is index 0. How much work does the app do to reach it, counting from the head?

options.k-moves: k moves, because the app follows k links from the head: O(n) at worst
options.one-move: 1 move, because the queue knows where each song is: O(1)
options.whole-queue: n moves, because the app always walks the whole queue: O(n)
options.halving: About log k moves, because the app can skip songs along the way

cost-of-reaching-index-k.explanation: The app follows k links from the head, so the cost grows with k and is O(n) in the worst case. A list cannot jump the way an array does, because nodes are not stored side by side. The walk stops at index k rather than at the end. A link only leads to the next node, so there is nothing to skip.

cheaper-on-a-list.prompt: Which job is cheaper on the linked list than on the array?

options.insert-after-current: Playing a song next, because only two links change and no song moves
options.read-by-index: Jumping to song 500, because the links lead straight to it
options.show-every-song: Showing every song in Up next, because each link leads to the next song

cheaper-on-a-list.explanation: Playing a song next is cheaper: two link changes on the list, O(1), while the array shifts every song behind it, O(n). Jumping to song 500 favours the array, with O(1) against a walk of 499 links. Showing every song costs O(n) on both, because each song is visited once either way.

linked-list.gloss: A chain of nodes where each node links to the next one and the last links to nothing.

node.gloss: One item of a linked list: a value plus a link to the next node.

head.gloss: The first node of a linked list, where every traversal starts.

pointer.gloss: A labelled marker that refers to one node, like now-playing or prev.

traversal.gloss: Visiting the nodes one after another by following their links.
